concepts.name: Constitutional Origin and Amendment History of Article 21A
key_dimensions: Inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 — not original Constitution
Simultaneous amendments to Article 45 (DPSP) and Article 51A(k) (Fundamental Duty) in the same amendment
Distinction: Article 21 (original) vs Article 21A (inserted) — trap on which article covers which right
RTE Act, 2009 enacted under Article 21A as the enabling legislation, not self-executing

concepts.name: Scope and Age Bracket: The '6-14 Years' Limitation
key_dimensions: Article 21A covers only children aged 6–14 years — UPSC trap on exclusion of under-6 and above-14
Pre-school (0–6 years) covered under Article 45 DPSP (early childhood care), NOT Article 21A
NEP 2020 proposes extending RTE to 3–18 years — contrast with current constitutional provision
Children with disabilities: RTE Act extends coverage up to 18 years as an exception to the 14-year ceiling

concepts.name: Nature of the Right: Justiciable Fundamental Right vs. DPSP
key_dimensions: Article 21A is a Fundamental Right (Part III) — enforceable in courts under Articles 32 and 226
Contrast with pre-2002 position: education was only in Article 45 DPSP (non-justiciable)
Unnikrishnan J.P. v. State of AP (1993) — SC read right to education into Article 21 before 86th Amendment
UPSC trap: Article 45 post-86th Amendment shifted focus to early childhood care, not elementary education

concepts.name: Right to Education Act (RTE) 2009: Key Structural Provisions
key_dimensions: Free and compulsory education — 'free' means no fees/charges; 'compulsory' is obligation on government, not child
No detention policy (Section 16) — controversial; amended in 2019 to allow detention after Class 5 and 8
No corporal punishment or mental harassment (Section 17) — penal consequences for violation
Neighbourhood school norm — government obligated to establish school within specified distance

concepts.name: 25% Reservation in Private Schools (Section 12(1)(c) of RTE Act)
key_dimensions: Unaided private schools must reserve 25% seats for EWS/disadvantaged children in entry-level class
Society of Unaided Private Schools v. Union of India (2012) — SC upheld 25% reservation; excluded minority institutions
Minority institutions (aided and unaided) exempted from 25% clause — Article 30 protection prevails
Reimbursement mechanism: government pays per-child cost to private schools for 25% reserved seats
UPSC trap: Aided minority schools are partially covered; unaided minority schools are fully exempt

concepts.name: Exclusion of Minority Institutions from RTE Act
key_dimensions: Both aided and unaided minority institutions exempted from the 25% reservation clause under Section 12(1)(c)
Constitutional basis: Article 30(1) — right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust v. Union of India (2014) — SC confirmed full exemption for unaided minority schools
UPSC trap: RTE applies to minority schools for other provisions (infrastructure, teacher norms) but NOT the 25% clause

concepts.name: Teacher Qualifications and Norms under RTE Act
key_dimensions: Section 23: academic and professional qualifications prescribed by academic authority (NCTE)
Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR) norms — 30:1 for Classes I–V; 35:1 for Classes VI–VIII
Deadline for untrained teachers to acquire qualifications — extended multiple times, most recently to 2019
Ban on deployment of teachers for non-educational purposes except decennial census, disaster relief, elections

concepts.name: No-Detention Policy and Its Amendment
key_dimensions: Original Section 16 of RTE: no child to be held back (detained) or expelled till completion of elementary education
RTE Amendment Act, 2019: states can conduct examinations at end of Class 5 and Class 8; detention possible on failing
Controversy: balance between 'joyful learning' and 'learning outcomes/accountability'
UPSC trap: No-detention policy is now discretionary for states, not a blanket prohibition

concepts.name: Infrastructure and School Standards under RTE Act (Schedule Norms)
key_dimensions: Schedule to RTE Act prescribes physical infrastructure: classrooms, toilets (separate for girls), drinking water, library
All schools had to meet norms within 3 years of RTE enactment (i.e., by 2013) — deadline largely missed
Schools not meeting norms can be de-recognized — UPSC trap on consequence of non-compliance
Mid-Day Meal scheme linked to RTE goals but governed by separate legislation/executive order

concepts.name: Prohibition on Screening and Capitation Fees
key_dimensions: Section 13: no school or person shall subject child/parent to screening procedure for admission
Section 13: no capitation fee shall be charged — penalty is 10 times the capitation fee amount
Lottery system mandated for admissions where seats are limited — no interviews, no donations
UPSC trap: prohibition applies to entry-level class admissions, not subsequent classes

concepts.name: Role of State vs. Central Government: Concurrent List Position
key_dimensions: Education is in the Concurrent List (List III, Entry 25) after the 42nd Amendment, 1976
Financial responsibility: Centre and States share — Centre bears 100% for UTs without legislature; 60:40 for general states; 90:10 for NE/special states
State governments responsible for implementation; Centre provides policy and financial support
UPSC trap: Before 42nd Amendment, education was in State List — significant shift in federal balance

concepts.name: Special Provisions for Disadvantaged Groups and Children with Disabilities
key_dimensions: RTE defines 'child belonging to disadvantaged group' — SC/ST, OBC, and other categories notified by state
Children with disabilities covered under RTE up to age 18 (exception to 6–14 bracket)
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPWD) intersects with RTE for inclusive education norms
Home-based education allowed for children with severe/multiple disabilities under RPWD, not mainstream RTE

concepts.name: School Management Committees (SMCs) under RTE
key_dimensions: Section 21: every government/aided school shall constitute an SMC — 75% members to be parents/guardians
SMC functions: monitor school working, prepare school development plans, utilize grants
Representation mandate: proportionate representation of disadvantaged/weaker section parents in SMC
UPSC trap: SMCs are mandatory for government and aided schools; private unaided schools have no SMC obligation under RTE

concepts.name: Judicial Evolution: From Mohini Jain to Unnikrishnan to Article 21A
key_dimensions: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992): SC held right to education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21 at all levels
Unnikrishnan J.P. v. State of AP (1993): SC restricted right to free education only up to age 14, linked to Article 45
Post-86th Amendment: constitutional text settled the debate — right now explicitly in Part III but only for 6–14
UPSC trap: Mohini Jain's broader interpretation (all levels) was diluted by Unnikrishnan and then constitutionally codified narrowly

concepts.name: Article 21A vs. Article 45 (DPSP): Post-86th Amendment Relationship
key_dimensions: Pre-2002: Article 45 directed state to provide free and compulsory education for all children up to age 14
Post-2002: Article 45 DPSP now covers early childhood care and education for children below 6 years
The shift created a two-tier structure: Article 21A (6–14, Fundamental Right) + Article 45 (0–6, DPSP)
UPSC trap: Article 45 no longer covers 6–14 education — a common reversal error in exams

concepts.name: Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k) and Its Correlation with Article 21A
key_dimensions: 86th Amendment also added Article 51A(k): parent/guardian duty to provide education to child between 6–14 years
This is the only Fundamental Duty that is correlative to a Fundamental Right (Article 21A)
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable but courts have used them as interpretive tools
UPSC trap: Duty is on parent/guardian, not on the child — and state's obligation remains primary

concepts.name: Application of RTE to Different Categories of Schools
key_dimensions: Four categories: (1) Government schools, (2) Aided private schools, (3) Unaided private schools, (4) Schools in specified category (cantonments, railways etc.)
25% EWS reservation applies differently: government schools admit fully; aided schools follow 25% norm; unaided non-minority schools must comply
Madrasas, Vedic pathshalas, and schools imparting only religious instruction are excluded from RTE Act
UPSC trap: 'Specified category schools' (KVs, Sainik Schools) have separate obligations under RTE

concepts.name: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and RTE Enforcement
key_dimensions: NCPCR designated as the national-level authority to monitor implementation of RTE Act (Section 31)
State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights (SCPCRs) perform state-level monitoring
Grievance redressal: complaints go to local authority → SCPCR → NCPCR in appellate hierarchy
UPSC trap: NCPCR is a statutory body under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 — not a constitutional body

concepts.name: NEP 2020 and Proposed Changes to the RTE Framework
key_dimensions: NEP 2020 proposes extending RTE coverage from 3–18 years (5+3+3+4 curricular structure) vs current 6–14
Emphasis on foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) for ages 3–8 — requires amending RTE Act
NEP recommends mother tongue/home language as medium of instruction up to Grade 5 — impacts RTE implementation norms
UPSC trap: NEP 2020 is a policy document, not law — RTE Act amendment needed to give NEP proposals legal force

concepts.name: RTE and Right Against Exploitation: Child Labour Intersection
key_dimensions: Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016: prohibits employment of children below 14 in any occupation
Alignment with RTE: both use the 14-year threshold, creating a mutually reinforcing legal framework
Article 24 (Fundamental Right): prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories/mines/hazardous employment
UPSC trap: Article 24 covers 'hazardous' work; post-2016 Child Labour Act expanded prohibition to ALL work for under-14 — broader than Article 24's text
